nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision metrology
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at a 'magic wavelength' so that the trapping light leaves the clock transition unshifted. This combines the high statistics of many atoms with the Lamb-Dicke confinement of a single ion. Ye turned the idea into metrology at the 10^-18 level. His group controlled many-body interactions in degenerate Fermi gases, imaged gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, and used frequency combs to compare clocks coherently. Katori's transportable clocks have measured geopotential differences, which opens relativistic geodesy. Together their work made optical frequency the most precisely measured quantity in physics. It is driving the redefinition of the SI second and enables searches for dark matter and for variation of fundamental constants. It is exactly the kind of tool that changes what can be measured across the whole of physics.
